extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys and agents subject to USPTO discipline (practitioners, OED staff, counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing registered patent practitioners' professional conduct before the USPTO, including duties to act diligently, keep clients informed, disclose third-party payments, and related disciplinary sanctions and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101-11.901)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are subject to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101 through 11.901); conduct occurring prior to May 3, 2013 is governed by the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20 to 10.112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order states that at all relevant times the Respondent was a registered patent attorney subject to these rules and that earlier conduct is governed by the prior Code. This orients which regulatory scheme applies to evaluate practitioner conduct in particular time frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Duty of Diligence and Promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the order: failing to promptly ascertain and execute the client's desired course of action after a Final Rejection (the '628 application), failing to respond or timely file an extension so that the application was abandoned, and failing to ascertain/execute the client's desired action after a Notice of Abandonment (the '386 application). These factual failures illustrate conduct that violates §11.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Ascertain and Execute Client's Desired Course of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must promptly ascertain the client's desired course of action and execute it when necessary to protect the client's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order repeatedly cites failures to 'promptly ascertain and execute the client's desired course of action' as misconduct (e.g., after Final Rejection and Notices of Abandonment). Specific misconduct examples: not determining client's instructions regarding response options, not filing responses or extensions that client might have chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f) — Accepting Compensation from One Other Than the Client (Third-Party Payments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must obtain informed consent when accepting compensation from a third party for representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order explains that accepting compensation from PSUS/PAW without obtaining the client's informed consent (including disclosure of material risks and reasonably available alternatives) violates §11.108(f). Examples: Respondent accepted payment from PSUS for legal opinions and filings without informing clients how much was paid to him or disclosing the relationship/terms; the March 2, 2011 warning similarly advised that consent after full disclosure is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Disclose Third-Party Payment Terms and Relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: When a third party pays a practitioner for services, the practitioner must disclose the relationship and payment terms to the client and obtain informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete failures noted: clients were not informed how much of the amounts they paid to PSUS was paid to the practitioner; the practitioner did not disclose his ongoing relationship, contractual terms, or significant payments from PSUS when issuing legal opinions or drafting applications. The order treats nondisclosure of third-party payment details as part of the §11.108(f) violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — Keep Client Reasonably Informed of Status
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order cites failure to inform Ms. Vincent and Mr. Audenby of Notices of Abandonment and other status developments (e.g., Notice to File Missing Parts) as violations of §11.104(a)(3). Example: Ms. Vincent discovered abandonment only by contacting the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4) — Promptly Comply with Reasonable Requests for Information
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must promptly comply with reasonable requests from the client for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order finds repeated failures to respond to Ms. Vincent's reasonable requests for status reports on applications are violations of §11.104(a)(4). Example: practitioner eventually stopped responding to the client's inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — Explain Matters Sufficiently for Informed Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must explain the matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order finds that not informing clients of notices of abandonment, failing to explain legal options going forward, and misrepresenting that necessary filings had been sent (when they had not) violated §11.104(b). Example: Respondent told Ms. Vincent she should not worry because he had sent what was needed, but he had taken no action.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.68(a)(1) (Code of Professional Responsibility) — Avoid Influence by Others Than the Client
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the pre-2013 Code, a practitioner must avoid being influenced by others than the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced in the March 2, 2011 warning letter: the practitioner was warned that accepting compensation from a referring company (PAW) could create improper influence; this historical citation frames earlier admonitions and the continuity of the duty to avoid third-party influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Communicate Directly with Client (not solely through Referrer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical communications (legal opinions, status notifications, options) should be communicated to the client and not routed exclusively through a third-party referrer such that the client is uninformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual example: Respondent emailed the legal opinion to PSUS (the referrer) rather than to the client and had no direct contact with the client before or after rendering legal opinions or drafting the provisional application. The order treats lack of direct client communication as contributing to violations of the disclosure, informed-consent, and notification duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to Respond to USPTO Office Actions and Fee Notices to Avoid Abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must ensure responses to USPTO Office Actions and payment of required fees (or timely extensions) are handled so client applications do not go abandoned without client knowledge and instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order details failures to respond to Non-Final and Final Rejections, not filing extensions, failing to pay fees in continuation-in-part (leading to Notice to File Missing Parts and abandonment), and not informing clients about these procedural matters. These procedural omissions are concrete examples of violating diligence and communication duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary Sanctions and Conditions (public reprimand, suspension, limited recognition, MPRE requirement, compliance with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate discipline for violations can include public reprimand, suspension (here, a 30‑month suspension), limited recognition to practice for specified purposes, and conditions for reinstatement such as passing the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE); practitioners must comply with relevant reinstatement and compliance regulations (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agreement and Final Order impose: a public reprimand for D2019-47; a 30-month suspension (D2017-11) with MPRE pass required prior to reinstatement; limited recognition for a narrow purpose and duration to facilitate compliance with §11.58(b); and an obligation to comply with the cited §§ 11.58 and 11.60. The order also notes that records of discipline may be considered in future proceedings as aggravating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and Public Access to Disciplinary Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary decisions and notices are published in the OED electronic FOIA reading room and in the Official Gazette (with notices materially consistent with the order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order requires electronic publication of the Final Order in the FOIA reading room and publication of a notice in the Official Gazette summarizing the discipline and the violations. This serves notice and transparency functions in practitioner discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional and Procedural Bases for Discipline (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32; 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19, 11.20, 11.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director and OED have jurisdiction to bring and approve disciplinary proceedings under statutory and regulatory authorities cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites these statutory/regulatory provisions as the basis for jurisdiction and authority to approve settlement agreements, issue final orders, and impose discipline; practitioners should be aware of these procedural authorities when assessing discipline processes.
